claim: Dynamic Organellar Maps is a proteomic method that allows global mapping of protein translocation events.
source: We have developed and applied Dynamic Organellar Maps, a proteomic method that allows global mapping of protein translocation events.
evidence: The abstract directly states the development and application of the method.

claim: The database contains localization and absolute copy number information for over 8700 proteins from HeLa cells.
source: We initially used maps statically to generate a database with localization and absolute copy number information for over 8700 proteins from HeLa cells, approaching comprehensive coverage.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative data on the number of proteins covered.

claim: All major organelles were resolved with exceptional prediction accuracy estimated at >92%.
source: All major organelles were resolved, with exceptional prediction accuracy (estimated at >92%).
evidence: The abstract provides a quantitative estimate of prediction accuracy.

claim: Protein function is critically determined by subcellular localization.
source: Protein function is critically determined by subcellular localization, as organelles offer different chemical environments and interaction partners.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Many biological processes involve changes in protein subcellular localization to regulate protein activity.
source: In order to regulate protein activity, many biological processes involve changes in protein subcellular localization.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Endocytic uptake of activated plasma membrane signalling receptors terminates the signalling process.
source: Prominent examples include the endocytic uptake of activated plasma membrane signalling receptors, to terminate the signalling process (Jones and Rappoport, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jones and Rappoport, 2014.

claim: Nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of many transcription factors regulates their access to DNA.
source: the nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling of many transcription factors, to regulate their access to DNA (Plotnikov et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Plotnikov et al., 2011.

claim: There is currently no proteomic method that allows global dynamic mapping of protein subcellular localization.
source: there is currently no proteomic method that allows global dynamic mapping of protein subcellular localization.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: High variability between spatial proteomics experiments renders the identification of genuine organellar transitions very difficult.
source: The main reason for this deficiency is the high variability between spatial proteomics experiments, which renders the identification of genuine organellar transitions very difficult (Gatto et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gatto et al., 2014.

claim: The fractionation profiling approach generates organellar profiles by high-accuracy quantification of each fraction against an invariant reference.
source: The principle of our approach is to separate organelles partially with a minimum number of fractionation steps, and to generate organellar profiles by high-accuracy quantification of each fraction against an invariant reference.
evidence: This describes the methodological principle of the approach.

claim: Metabolically labelled HeLa cells (SILAC light or heavy) were mechanically lysed following gentle hypo-osmotic swelling.
source: Metabolically labelled HeLa cells, SILAC light or heavy (Ong et al., 2002), were mechanically lysed following gentle hypo-osmotic swelling (Figure 1A).
evidence: The text describes the experimental procedure and references Figure 1A.

claim: Damage to organelles was minimal, as assessed by leakage of lumenal contents.
source: Damage to organelles was minimal, as assessed by leakage of lumenal contents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The fractionation procedure is highly reproducible, as assessed by protein recovery.
source: This procedure is highly reproducible, as assessed by protein recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: In a typical experiment, approximately 4500 proteins were profiled.
source: In a typical experiment, approximately 4500 proteins were profiled.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the experimental output.

claim: Proteins associated with the same organelle have similar profiles, and organelles can be distinguished from one another.
source: Proteins associated with the same organelle have similar profiles, and organelles can be distinguished from one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The global distributions of proteins across nuclear, organellar, and cytosolic fractions were obtained by label-free quantification mass-spectrometry, typically covering 8000 proteins.
source: In parallel, the global distributions of proteins across the nuclear, organellar, and cytosolic fractions were obtained by label-free quantification mass-spectrometry, typically covering 8000 proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text describes the method and quantitative output, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Six replicate fractionations were prepared in batches of two, on three different days.
source: Following this scheme, we prepared six replicate fractionations, in batches of two, on three different days.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Principal component analysis was applied to the abundance profiles of 3766 proteins common to all replicates.
source: We first considered the set of 3766 proteins common to all replicates, and applied principal component analysis (PCA) to their abundance profiles.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach.

claim: Resolved compartments included plasma membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, ERGIC, Golgi apparatus, endosome, lysosome, peroxisomes and mitochondria, as well as a cluster of diverse large protein complexes.
source: Resolved compartments included plasma membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, ERGIC, Golgi apparatus, endosome, lysosome, peroxisomes and mitochondria, as well as a cluster of diverse large protein complexes, such as ribosomes and proteasomes.
evidence: This describes the organellar compartments resolved by the method.

claim: The organellar maps show partial sub-organellar resolution, revealing a divide between ER membrane and lumen, as well as division of mitochondria into matrix, inner membrane, and outer membrane.
source: Closer inspection of the marker proteins suggested further sub-organellar resolution, revealing a partial divide between ER membrane and lumen, as well as division of mitochondria into matrix, inner membrane, and outer membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UniProt annotation for subcellular targeting features showed near-complete agreement with the organellar maps.
source: For independent validation, we overlaid the scores plot with UniProt annotation for subcellular targeting features, including signal peptides, mitochondrial transit peptides and transmembrane domains, and observed near-complete agreement with our maps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with external annotations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All six individual maps had very similar patterns with organellar clusters occupying stable positions between maps.
source: To assess the reproducibility of the method, we next analysed the six individual maps by PCA; all had very similar patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), with organellar clusters occupying stable positions between maps.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The SILAC ratios of replicate fractions were highly reproducible with average correlation > 0.95.
source: The SILAC ratios of replicate fractions were also highly reproducible (average correlation > 0.95; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A support vector machine (SVM)-based supervised learning approach was used for rigorous assignment of proteins to organellar clusters.
source: For the rigorous assignment of proteins to organellar clusters, we used a support vector machine (SVM)-based supervised learning approach.
evidence: This describes the computational method used for classification.

claim: A canonical set of over 1000 organellar markers was manually curated.
source: Since a suitable canonical set of organellar markers was not available, we manually curated a set of over 1000 proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the creation of a marker set for the analysis.

claim: The mean prediction accuracy for marker proteins was 94.7% with full cross validation.
source: We applied SVM classification to all six maps individually. The mean prediction accuracy for marker proteins was 94.7% (with full cross validation), demonstrating the exceptionally high level of organellar resolution achieved (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of prediction accuracy from the SVM analysis.

claim: The average proportion of identical organellar assignments between maps (concordance) was 93.7% for all proteins, and >98% for three-quarters of the proteins.
source: The average proportion of identical organellar assignments between maps, referred to as concordance, was 93.7% for all proteins, and >98% for three-quarters of the proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of reproducibility shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Fractionation profiling is effective for generating high resolution organellar maps with remarkable reproducibility enabling comparative applications.
source: Collectively, these data show that fractionation profiling is effective for generating high resolution organellar maps. The remarkable level of reproducibility enables comparative applications (see below).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the presented data.

claim: Organellar profiles were derived for 5265 proteins, of which 2423 were assigned to 9 membranous organelles.
source: In total, we derived organellar profiles for 5265 proteins, of which 2423 were assigned to 9 membranous organelles, with 96.5% of marker proteins predicted correctly (92.7% average per membrane-bound organelle; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the prediction output.

claim: 96.5% of marker proteins were predicted correctly overall, with 92.7% average per membrane-bound organelle.
source: In total, we derived organellar profiles for 5265 proteins, of which 2423 were assigned to 9 membranous organelles, with 96.5% of marker proteins predicted correctly (92.7% average per membrane-bound organelle; Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of prediction accuracy.

claim: For eight of the nine compartments, the most significantly enriched UniProt localization term corresponded to the organellar classification.
source: To validate the novel predictions, we removed the organellar markers from the set, and annotated the remaining proteins with UniProt subcellular localization information. A Fisher's exact test showed that for eight of the nine compartments, the most significantly enriched localization term corresponded to our own organellar classification (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes validation using external annotations and statistical testing.

claim: The overall concordance with the MitoCarta database of experimentally validated mitochondrial proteins was 97% (92.3% for non-marker proteins).
source: Furthermore, we compared our mitochondrial predictions with the MitoCarta database of experimentally validated mitochondrial proteins (Calvo et al., 2016); the overall concordance was 97% (92.3% for non-marker proteins).
evidence: This describes validation using an external database with citation to Calvo et al., 2016.

claim: The global profile analysis extends to 8710 proteins, including 1999 cytosolic, 1133 nuclear, and 672 nucleo-cytosolic proteins.
source: In total, this global profile analysis extends to 8710 proteins, including 1999 cytosolic, 1133 nuclear, and 672 nucleo-cytosolic proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the global profile analysis.

claim: The endomembrane system contributes approximately 16% to total cellular protein mass.
source: This revealed that the endomembrane system contributes approximately 16% to total cellular protein mass, dominated by mitochondria (6.6%), ER (4.4%), and plasma membrane (3.1%), with relatively minor contributions from endosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes and Golgi (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation based on the data, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mitochondria contribute 6.6% to total cellular protein mass.
source: This revealed that the endomembrane system contributes approximately 16% to total cellular protein mass, dominated by mitochondria (6.6%), ER (4.4%), and plasma membrane (3.1%), with relatively minor contributions from endosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes and Golgi (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ER contributes 4.4% to total cellular protein mass.
source: This revealed that the endomembrane system contributes approximately 16% to total cellular protein mass, dominated by mitochondria (6.6%), ER (4.4%), and plasma membrane (3.1%), with relatively minor contributions from endosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes and Golgi (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Plasma membrane contributes 3.1% to total cellular protein mass.
source: This revealed that the endomembrane system contributes approximately 16% to total cellular protein mass, dominated by mitochondria (6.6%), ER (4.4%), and plasma membrane (3.1%), with relatively minor contributions from endosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes and Golgi (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 20 most abundant proteins constitute at least 40% of organellar protein mass in mitochondria, ER and plasma membrane.
source: In each case, the 20 most abundant proteins constitute at least 40% of organellar protein mass (Figure 3C–E, and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: The most abundant plasma membrane protein is the 4F2 cell-surface antigen heavy chain (SLC3A2), with 15 million copies/cell.
source: For example, the most abundant plasma membrane protein is the 4F2 cell-surface antigen heavy chain (SLC3A2), with 15 million copies/cell.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of protein abundance.

claim: All plasma membrane transporters combined (40 million copies) contribute approximately 25% of the total compartment protein mass.
source: Supporting this view, all plasma membrane transporters combined (40 million copies) contribute approximately 25% of the total compartment protein mass.
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation of protein mass contribution.

claim: The estimated density of integral membrane proteins at the plasma membrane is 4–5 per 100 nm2.
source: Assuming a cell surface area of ~1600 μm2 typical of adherent HeLa cells (Fisher and Cooper, 1967) yields an estimated density of 4–5 integral membrane proteins per 100 nm2, in excellent agreement with a previous biochemically derived estimate of 3 for baby hamster kidney (BHK) fibroblasts (Quinn et al., 1984).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data, with citations to Fisher and Cooper, 1967 and Quinn et al., 1984 for comparison.

claim: Within the endoplasmic reticulum, proteins involved in protein folding and quality control predominate (20% chaperones, 10% protein disulfide isomerases).
source: Within the endoplasmic reticulum, proteins involved in protein folding and quality control predominate (20% chaperones, 10% protein disulfide isomerases).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of ER protein composition.

claim: Chaperones constitute 14% of mitochondrial protein mass.
source: A similar abundance of chaperones was observed in the mitochondria (14%), which exceeds the collective contribution of citric acid cycle components (9%).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of mitochondrial protein composition.

claim: The number of mitochondrial ATP synthase F0 complexes is estimated at ~3 million per cell (5% of mitochondrial protein mass).
source: We detected the five members of the mitochondrial ATP synthase F0 catalytic complex with the expected stoichiometry of ~3:1 for subunits A/B to C/D/E, and estimate the number of complexes at ~3 million per cell (5% of mitochondrial protein mass).
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on the data.

claim: Following EGF stimulation, EGFR autophosphorylates, binds downstream factors, and is rapidly endocytosed from the plasma membrane to an endosomal compartment.
source: Following stimulation with EGF, EGFR autophosphorylates, binds downstream factors, and is rapidly endocytosed from the plasma membrane to an endosomal compartment (Jones and Rappoport, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citation to Jones and Rappoport, 2014.

claim: EGFR localized to the plasma membrane cluster in control cells and to the endosomal cluster upon EGF treatment.
source: Overall map morphology from treated and control cells was unchanged, however EGFR, which localized to the plasma membrane cluster in control cells, was localized to the endosomal cluster upon EGF treatment, as expected.
evidence: This describes the observed translocation in the organellar maps.

claim: Four proteins were identified as significantly translocating with stringent FDR control: EGFR, GRB2, SHC1 and PKN2.
source: Applying these cut-offs to the EGF treatment experiment identified four proteins as significantly translocating; EGFR, GRB2, SHC1 and PKN2.
evidence: This is the result of the statistical analysis of translocation events.

claim: GRB2 and SHC1 are recruited to EGFR upon EGF stimulation and constitute the first step in EGFR signaling.
source: Both GRB2 and SHC1 are recruited to EGFR upon EGF stimulation and constitute the first step in EGFR signaling (Oda et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge with citation to Oda et al., 2005.

claim: All four significantly translocating proteins (EGFR, GRB2, SHC1, PKN2) moved to the endosome/lysosomal compartment.
source: Inspection of the maps (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and classification with support vector machines (Supplementary file 6) showed that all proteins had moved to the endosome/lysosomal compartment, as expected.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the maps shown in Figures 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: With relaxed score cut-offs allowing an FDR of 10%, 14 further significantly translocating proteins were identified.
source: For a deeper exploratory analysis, we then relaxed score cut-offs to allow an FDR of 10%, and identified 14 further significantly translocating proteins (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This describes the results of a less stringent analysis.

claim: The 14 additional translocating proteins included numerous known downstream targets of EGF, such as RPS6KA3, PIK3C2B and ROCK2, as well as several new candidates.
source: These included numerous known downstream targets of EGF, such as RPS6KA3, PIK3C2B and ROCK2, as well as several new candidates (see Discussion).
evidence: This describes the identity of the additional translocating proteins.

claim: 26 significant changes in protein abundance in membrane, nuclear and cytosolic fractions were identified following EGF stimulation.
source: Stringent FDR controls were derived using a mock experiment of our six database maps, as above, identifying 26 significant changes in the EGF experiment (Supplementary file 7, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is the result of the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Substantial recruitment of GRB2 and SHC1 to membranes was detected following EGF stimulation.
source: In agreement with the organellar maps, we detected substantial recruitment of GRB2 and SHC1 to membranes.
evidence: This is based on the global profile analysis.

claim: Recruitment of CBL and UBASH3B to membranes was observed following EGF stimulation.
source: In addition, we observed recruitment of CBL and UBASH3B, which are also known to bind to activated EGFR (Grovdal et al., 2004; Raguz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on the data, with citations to Grovdal et al., 2004 and Raguz et al., 2007 for validation.

claim: CBL and UBASH3B were not detected in control maps but were found in individual EGF-treated maps in the endosome/lysosome.
source: Consistent with that, CBL and UBASH3B were not detected in control maps but were found in individual EGF-treated maps, in the endosome/lysosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the maps shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The known translocation of RPS6KA3 into the nucleus was identified following EGF stimulation.
source: Among others, we identified the known translocation of RPS6KA3 into the nucleus, as well as a surprising number of transcriptional regulators leaving the nucleus (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on the global profile analysis.

claim: A surprising number of transcriptional regulators were observed leaving the nucleus following EGF stimulation.
source: Among others, we identified the known translocation of RPS6KA3 into the nucleus, as well as a surprising number of transcriptional regulators leaving the nucleus (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on the global profile analysis.

claim: ZCCHC8 and RBM7, the unique components of the nuclear exosome targeting (NEXT) complex, were among the transcriptional regulators leaving the nucleus.
source: These included ZCCHC8 and RBM7, the unique components of the nuclear exosome targeting (NEXT) complex (Lubas et al., 2011), which targets the exosome to promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTS) for their degradation.
evidence: This is based on the data, with citation to Lubas et al., 2011.

claim: The data suggest that EGF may induce modulation of the non-coding transcriptome.
source: Therefore our data suggest that EGF may induce modulation of the non-coding transcriptome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed nuclear export of NEXT complex components.

claim: There is a significant overall loss of EGFR upon EGF treatment (from 700,000 to 620,000 copies per cell, p=0.0022).
source: For example, our data show a significant overall loss of EGFR upon EGF treatment (from 700,000 to 620,000 copies per cell, p=0.0022), suggesting that a proportion of endocytosed EGFR has already been degraded in lysosomes.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical significance.

claim: Approximately 500,000 copies of GRB2 are recruited onto endosomes/EGFR, suggesting a stoichiometry of ~1:1 with EGFR.
source: Approximately 500,000 copies of GRB2 are recruited onto endosomes/EGFR, suggesting a stoichiometry of ~1:1 with EGFR.
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation based on the data.

claim: CBL (10,000 copies) and UBASH3B (30,000 copies) are recruited sub-stoichiometrically to EGFR.
source: In contrast, CBL (10,000 copies) and UBASH3B (30,000 copies) are recruited sub-stoichiometrically, as would be expected of enzymatically acting proteins.
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation with interpretation based on known protein function.

claim: SHC1 (100,000 copies) is recruited sub-stoichiometrically to EGFR.
source: SHC1 (100,000 copies) is also recruited sub-stoichiometrically.
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation based on the data.

claim: The cell loses three quarters of its Vasorin (30,000 copies), most likely through plasma membrane shedding.
source: The cell loses three quarters of its Vasorin (a negative regulator of TGFB signalling; 30,000 copies), most likely through plasma membrane shedding (Malapeira et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation with interpretation based on citation to Malapeira et al., 2011.

claim: Over 300,000 copies of the actin regulator Palladin are released into the cytosol following EGF stimulation.
source: Over 300,000 copies of the actin regulator Palladin are released into the cytosol, and the Rho-effector PKN2 is shifted to endosomes, indicating major cytoskeletal rearrangements.
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation based on the data.

claim: The Rho-effector PKN2 is shifted to endosomes following EGF stimulation, indicating major cytoskeletal rearrangements.
source: Over 300,000 copies of the actin regulator Palladin are released into the cytosol, and the Rho-effector PKN2 is shifted to endosomes, indicating major cytoskeletal rearrangements.
evidence: This is based on the data with interpretation.

claim: Localization information is provided for 8710 proteins in HeLa cells.
source: Here, we provide localization information for 8710 proteins in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the database content.

claim: The complexity of the HeLa proteome has been estimated at around 10,000 proteins.
source: The complexity of the HeLa proteome has been estimated at around 10,000 proteins (Beck et al., 2011; Nagaraj et al., 2011); a substantial proportion of this is covered by our database.
evidence: This is a statement based on citations to Beck et al., 2011 and Nagaraj et al., 2011.

claim: The database accounts for the vast majority of protein cell mass.
source: Importantly, it accounts for the vast majority of protein cell mass (as can for example be seen from the cumulative mass plots in Figure 3B, which all reach a stable plateau)
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fractionation protocol is five times faster than the previous LOPIT approach (4 hr vs ~20 hr).
source: Relative to the previous LOPIT approach (localization of organelle proteins by isotope tagging; Christoforou et al., 2016), our fractionation protocol is five times faster (4 hr vs ~20 hr), and requires an order of magnitude less starting material (107 cells vs 108 cells).
evidence: This is a comparison with the LOPIT method cited as Christoforou et al., 2016.

claim: The fractionation protocol requires an order of magnitude less starting material than LOPIT (107 cells vs 108 cells).
source: Relative to the previous LOPIT approach (localization of organelle proteins by isotope tagging; Christoforou et al., 2016), our fractionation protocol is five times faster (4 hr vs ~20 hr), and requires an order of magnitude less starting material (107 cells vs 108 cells).
evidence: This is a comparison with the LOPIT method cited as Christoforou et al., 2016.

claim: 2397 homologous proteins were classified in both this study and a recent LOPIT analysis of mouse stem cells, of which 2196 had identical compartment predictions (91.6%).
source: Furthermore, we made a direct comparison with a recent analysis of the mouse stem cell spatial proteome using LOPIT (Christoforou et al., 2016). 2397 homologous proteins were classified in both studies, of which 2196 had identical compartment predictions (91.6%; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with external data from Christoforou et al., 2016.

claim: Comparison to 'gold standard' quantification with isotope labelled peptides (PrEST approach) shows similar precision for the proteomic ruler approach, with typical absolute deviations of less than two-fold.
source: The proteomic ruler approach is remarkably accurate; comparison to 'gold standard' quantification with isotope labelled peptides (PrEST approach [Zeiler et al., 2012]) shows similar precision, and typical absolute deviations of less than two-fold (Wisniewski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the accuracy of the proteomic ruler method with citations to Zeiler et al., 2012 and Wisniewski et al., 2014.

claim: The average Pearson correlation of copy numbers between replicates was 0.98.
source: To assess the quality of our analysis, we first compared the prediction consistency from the individual Static Maps (six biological replicates). The average Pearson correlation of copy numbers between replicates was 0.98 (calculated from 15 pairwise comparisons, log data), demonstrating very high precision (ie prediction reproducibility).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of reproducibility.

claim: Pearson correlation of copy numbers from this study with PrEST data was 0.96.
source: To gauge prediction accuracy, we compared median copy numbers predicted from our maps with absolute copy numbers of 27 proteins derived in an independent study using the PrEST approach (Zeiler et al., 2012). Pearson correlation of the two datasets (in log space) was 0.96, and thus remarkably high, showing a near-linear relationship of our data with the PrEST data.
evidence: This is a comparison with external data from Zeiler et al., 2012.

claim: Leakage was 3.9% for mitochondria, 2.3% for lysosomes, and 8.3% for ER.
source: We therefore calculated the averages from proteins with cytosolic pools between 1–20% only, indicating leakage of 3.9% for mitochondria, 2.3% for lysosomes, and 8.3% for ER.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of organellar leakage.

claim: These very low leakage values suggest that organelles are largely intact.
source: These values suggest a very high level of organellar integrity achieved by our lysis procedure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the leakage data.

claim: The analysis identified ten major regulators of actin dynamics following EGF stimulation.
source: In total, our analysis identified 40 translocation events, including numerous previously unreported movements. Among them are ten major regulators of actin dynamics, such as the kinases ROCK2, PKN2, PIK3C2B, and their downstream targets ADD1 and CTNN1, as well as PALLD, LASP1, and UTRN, suggesting that re-arrangement of the cytoskeleton is one of the major immediate effects of EGF signalling in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the identified translocating proteins.

claim: Re-arrangement of the cytoskeleton is one of the major immediate effects of EGF signalling in HeLa cells.
source: Among them are ten major regulators of actin dynamics, such as the kinases ROCK2, PKN2, PIK3C2B, and their downstream targets ADD1 and CTNN1, as well as PALLD, LASP1, and UTRN, suggesting that re-arrangement of the cytoskeleton is one of the major immediate effects of EGF signalling in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identified translocating proteins.

claim: For several actin dynamics proteins, this study provides the first experimental evidence that they are targets of the EGF pathway.
source: For several of these proteins, this study provides the first experimental evidence that they are targets of the EGF pathway (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is a statement about novel findings.

claim: Vasorin-shedding, AHNK and PDCD4 rerouting are all likely to counteract anti-proliferative TGFB signalling.
source: Our data also reveal an unexpected cross-talk with other signalling pathways; Vasorin-shedding, AHNK and PDCD4 rerouting are all likely to counteract anti-proliferative TGFB signalling, and may serve to enhance EGF activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed changes.

claim: Nuclear protein export has been reported comparatively rarely compared to nuclear import.
source: While nuclear import of proteins, such as ERK2/MAPK1, is a common downstream effect of signalling, nuclear protein export has been reported comparatively rarely.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Protein import concentrates the signal in the nucleus, whereas export diffuses it, making export more difficult to detect with conventional approaches such as microscopy.
source: A possible explanation is that this type of movement is more difficult to detect with conventional approaches, such as microscopy: protein import concentrates the signal in the nucleus, whereas export diffuses it.
evidence: This is an inference about why nuclear export is less commonly reported.

claim: Dynamic organellar maps identify the co-ordinated behaviour of functionally linked groups of proteins, uncovering cellular response modules.
source: Taken together, these observations highlight the power of the holistic proteomic approach, which identifies the co-ordinated behaviour of functionally linked groups of proteins, and thus uncovers cellular response modules.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the capabilities of the method.

claim: Dynamic organellar maps will be suitable for studying autophagy, membrane trafficking and cellular differentiation.
source: We propose that they will be similarly suitable in the fields of autophagy, membrane trafficking and cellular differentiation, providing a powerful complement to imaging-based techniques.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: Dynamic organellar maps offer an unbiased approach to studying cellular dynamics that does not require prior knowledge.
source: Since they offer an unbiased approach to studying cellular dynamics that does not require prior knowledge, they will also be an effective tool for exploratory investigations of poorly characterized processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the method.

claim: Combining organellar maps with high-throughput phosphoproteomics data promises to provide unprecedented views of signalling.
source: The possibility to combine maps with high-throughput phosphoproteomics data (Humphrey et al., 2015) promises to provide unprecedented views of signalling, by linking the movement of substrates to their phosphorylation status.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications with citation to Humphrey et al., 2015.

claim: Organellar maps will pave the way for quantitative process modelling in cell biology.
source: Moreover, as we have shown here, organellar maps will pave the way for quantitative process modelling in cell biology.
evidence: This is a statement about the future impact of the method.
